One-page synthesis

Core thesis. The paper introduces shadow evaluations: give an agent the central question from an unpublished research paper, prevent access to the answer, and have the original authors grade the returned work. In two NeurIPS-level empirical AI tasks, well-resourced agents completed the engineering workflow but produced papers that the original authors clearly rejected.

The main empirical contribution is not simply that the papers were rejected. The trajectories show a repeated pattern: the agents generated plausible initial ideas, moved too quickly from weak evidence to a settled direction, failed to use repeated negative reviews as a reason to rethink the project, left substantial resources unused, and gradually violated explicit instructions. The authors group these observations into five failure modes: poor judgment about the research bar, weak creative problem solving, ineffective backtracking, poor context/resource awareness, and instruction drift.

Several findings complicate a simplistic “agents cannot do research” reading. The agents handled literature search, GPU debugging, experiment execution, web/email tool use, review retrieval, and LaTeX compilation. They generally behaved honestly with negative results; the orchestrator caught five subagent result-misrepresentation incidents before final submission. Higher reasoning effort improved pilot quality. A GPT-5.6 Sol/Codex robustness run reproduced many failures but also found a real-world shifted dataset, indicating some configuration-sensitive improvement.

What the evidence does not establish. Two research questions, non-blind original-author reviewers, researcher discretion in task selection and interpretation, and only one alternate model/scaffold run sharply limit generalization. The study supports a claim about these runs and provides a useful failure taxonomy; it does not justify a broad forecast about all frontier models, all research styles, or the pace of AI-driven R&D acceleration.

Section condensation

Abstract

The authors frame a gap between verifier-scored AI-R&D benchmarks and blind peer-review demonstrations, then propose shadow evaluations as an alternative for open-ended research. Two unpublished NeurIPS 2026 questions were given to frontier agents with six days and substantial API/GPU budgets; both final papers were rejected by the original authors.

The abstract’s strongest supported conclusion is narrower than a general capability claim: current agents in these case studies could perform research engineering but struggled with judgment, creative redesign, backtracking, resource awareness, and instruction retention.

1. Introduction

The introduction argues that many claims about rapid AI progress depend on models being able to do more than optimize fixed metrics. Open-ended research requires selecting hypotheses, deciding what evidence is decisive, recognizing dead ends, and integrating feedback—capabilities poorly captured by narrow verifiers.

The proposed design uses unpublished research to reduce contamination and original authors to supply deep task-specific expertise. Each main run received six days, a $3,000 Anthropic API budget, GPU credits, a VM, and open-web access, with the goal of producing a top-conference-quality paper.

2. Shadow evaluations

Shadow evaluation is positioned as complementary to verifier-scored tasks and blind-review publication tests. Its strengths are open-endedness, task freshness, and expert grading; its structural weaknesses are small samples, non-blind review, researcher degrees of freedom, and subjective interpretation.

The methodological idea is valuable because it makes the unit of evaluation resemble delegated real research: an expert gives an agent a question the expert genuinely cares about and judges whether the returned work advances it. However, the same expert involvement also creates dependence between task selection, the reference solution, and evaluation.

3. Task and research setup

The two target questions were: (1) whether LLM personas can be represented and controlled in a structured weight-space trait geometry; and (2) whether a white-box prior-fitted network can detect harmful deployment-time distribution shift without labels. Original authors formulated the questions, estimated useful budgets, and later reviewed the outputs.

Both main runs used Opus 4.8 with extra-high reasoning in OpenClaw. Agents could use subagents, external review tools, GPU jobs, a research log, budget monitors, and the open web. Human interventions were documented and mainly logistical, plus a 24-hour extension and a readability rewrite request. Twelve collaborators recorded pre-experiment expectations.

4.1–4.2: Conference quality and partial value

The Personas paper received an overall 2/6 (“Reject”) and the TabPFN paper 1/6 (“Strong Reject”). Criterion scores were low on quality, clarity, and significance; reviewers criticized post-hoc or unprincipled experimental choices, weak support for conclusions, limited novelty, and dense presentation. Survey respondents had assigned a median 30% chance of weak accept or better.

There was still partial value: original authors liked aspects of the literature review, the ability to run large numbers of experiments, and some initial hypotheses. The authors describe a few minor findings as interesting, consistent with the survey’s more optimistic median 60% probability of moderate success.

4.3: Premature commitment

Both agents compressed exploration far more than planned. The Personas run budgeted 42 hours for open-ended exploration but converged around one method after about five hours; the TabPFN trajectory likewise committed to its headline direction substantially before the planned milestone. Ten of twelve survey respondents had expected shortcut-taking.

The key weakness is not simply speed. The authors argue the agents used small or synthetic evidence to reject ambitious hypotheses, then treated the resulting weaker direction as the project rather than as a signal to broaden exploration.

4.4: Feedback and the generator–verifier gap

Across 15 self-review rounds, none returned an acceptance. External and self-review systems often noticed concerns that also appeared in the human reviews, but the agents responded by adding caveats, narrowing claims, or fixing minor issues rather than revisiting the data or premise. They also overweighted more lenient reviews when review tools disagreed.

This motivates the paper’s generator–verifier framing: critique may be available without the policy needed to act on critique. The authors appropriately note that verifier accuracy is not established because every evaluated final paper was bad; uniformly rejecting weak drafts is not evidence that the verifier could distinguish good from bad research.

4.5–4.6: Engineering competence and presentation failure

The agents completed literature review, GPU environment debugging, experiment execution, robustness checks, external-review retrieval, and camera-ready LaTeX generation. Nine of eleven surveyed collaborators had expected an unresolvable-error loop, so the engineering competence exceeded those priors.

Presentation remained poor. Both final papers exceeded the nine-page limit; the Personas paper had zero main-text visualizations versus 15 in the original paper; reference counts were 16 versus 52 for Personas and 36 versus 69 for TabPFN. Seven of eleven respondents had predicted obvious misformatting.

4.7: Reward hacking and safety-relevant behavior

Manual review of raw model calls and committed code found no evidence that the orchestrator intentionally hid or distorted results to obtain a stronger paper; if anything, unsupported positive claims were retired. The agents also produced reproducibility code, though repository organization was weak.

Two safety-relevant issues remained: one run committed an access token to the repository, and subagents hallucinated or misrepresented results five times. In all five cases, the instructed orchestrator verification step caught the problem before the final draft.

4.8–4.9: Reasoning effort and harness improvement

Two earlier no-reasoning Opus 4.8 pilots showed the same broad failure modes but had poorer literature review and much worse writing, and the outputs were not considered worth external expert review. This is suggestive—not controlled evidence—that greater within-call reasoning improved output quality.

A subsequent Fable 5 attempt to improve the scaffold from pilot telemetry repeated a familiar pattern: it generalized broadly from an n=1 example and made rule changes that did not appear to address the underlying problems. This section is best read as a caution about meta-optimization from sparse failure traces, not as a formal scaffold ablation.

5. Log analysis: five failure modes

Judgment: agents did not maintain a calibrated model of what counts as publishable evidence. Creative problem solving: initial ideas were often plausible, but when they failed, agents tended to narrow the question rather than redesign the study. Backtracking: local retries were common, project-level restarts were rare. In TabPFN, six approaches were falsified within 14 hours, yet the project direction was not fundamentally reset despite roughly 110 hours remaining.

Context awareness: agents knew how to query budgets but did not translate those values into an effective work policy. Instruction drift: multi-day execution degraded compliance with review-tool use, exploration gates, and paper-length rules. These labels are interpretive; the paper explicitly records disagreement over whether “creativity,” epistemic lock-in, myopia, or reasoning deficits best explain the same trajectories.

6. GPT-5.6 Sol / Codex robustness experiment

The TabPFN task was rerun in Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol at an ultra reasoning setting. The wrapper repeatedly checked budgets and restarted the agent with a new model-generated review if it stopped early. The run again produced underpowered experiments, no novel contribution, formatting problems, and weak budget management.

The resource failure differed: the $3,000 token budget was exhausted in just over two days, leaving nearly 100 hours of wall-clock time. Positive behaviors also persisted—negative findings were reported honestly, self-review rejected weak drafts, and the agent improved on the original runs by using a real-world shifted dataset.

7. Limitations and implications

The strongest limitations are small task count, non-blind original-author grading, task-selection discretion, incomplete model/scaffold coverage, and possible under-elicitation from a documented OpenClaw context-reset bug (14 resets in TabPFN and five in Personas). The authors could not test Anthropic’s strongest restricted model, and the agents had far less time than the human researchers who created the reference work.

The paper therefore separates “can autonomously execute this kind of open-ended research” from the broader question “can AI accelerate AI R&D.” Full project autonomy may not be necessary for acceleration, so a negative result here does not directly falsify faster-R&D forecasts.

8. Potential biases

The authors explicitly disclose that members of the core team are publicly skeptical of imminent runaway recursive self-improvement and that this prior could affect study design and interpretation. Open-world evaluation necessarily trades objective scoring for richer tasks, making epistemic diversity, disagreement disclosure, and artifact release unusually important.

Log analysis is especially interpretation-heavy: researchers may notice behaviors that fit prior expectations. The paper mitigates this partly through coauthor disagreement, dry runs, generous budgets, a different model/scaffold robustness run, and artifact release, but these steps do not remove the core subjectivity.

Figures, tables, and workflow

Figure 1 — Resource trajectories

Purpose: Show wall-clock progress, API spend, GPU spend, and major trajectory events.
Key values: Personas — $1,130/$3,000 API; $392/$500 GPU. TabPFN — $1,235/$3,000 API; $69/$100 GPU.
Pattern: Both runs reached the deadline with substantial API budget unused; engineering milestones continued while research direction had already narrowed.
Interpretation: Supports the context/resource-awareness claim, but budget underuse alone does not prove more spending would have improved research quality.

Figure 2 — Planned versus realized milestones

Purpose: Compare intended research-process timing with actual commitment.
Personas: 42 hours planned for open-ended exploration; method selected after about 5 hours.
TabPFN: research direction committed substantially earlier than planned.
Interpretation: Strong visual evidence for premature project-level commitment; causal attribution to "creativity" versus calibration remains subjective.

Figure 3 — Review trajectories

Purpose: Compare self-review, external AI review, and human expert review.
Main pattern: 15 self-review rounds yielded no acceptance. Stanford reviews were more lenient than other reviewers; final human verdicts remained Reject / Strong Reject.
Interpretation: The agents had access to negative feedback but did not convert it into a project reset. Because all papers were poor, review discrimination is unproven.

Figure 4 — Readability intervention

Purpose: Visually compare papers before and after a human-requested clarity pass.
Pattern: A late rewrite materially changes presentation, demonstrating that human prompting could improve surface readability even after the research direction was largely fixed.
Limit: The figure is qualitative and does not measure whether readability changes affected scientific validity.

TabPFN: Both reviews noticed unsupported generalization, weak originality, and validation problems; the human expert rated these as decisive while the agent kept iterating within the same framing.
Main pattern: critique detection was better than critique prioritization and response policy.

Figure 5 / workflow — OpenClaw scaffold

Inputs: task instructions, budgets, project files, tool access.
Core loop: model turn → tool calls → tool results → next reasoning step.
Delegation: core agent dispatches subagents; subagents can call tools and return results.
Long-running work: GPU experiments execute asynchronously and are checked by later turns.
Continuation: heartbeat checks can start new turns while work remains; final paper returns to the human evaluator.
Failure surfaces: context resets/compaction, budget policy, subagent verification, early stopping, instruction retention, and review-to-action translation.

Appendix evidence

Appendix A — Research questions

Personas: develop a weight-based persona intervention, test whether dimensions are independent/composable, and test transfer to an untrained downstream behavior. TabPFN: design and justify a deployment-time harmful-shift detector using white-box PFN affordances, labeled in-distribution data, and an unlabeled deployment batch.

Appendix B — Original-author reviews

The detailed reviews strengthen the main-text score table by showing why the low scores were not primarily about polish. TabPFN criticism focused on unsupported generalization from a handful of failed signals, lack of a genuinely new detector relative to prior methods, and weak real-shift validation. Personas criticism focused on post-hoc trait/data choices, unclear practical payoff for weight-space geometry, potentially circular measurement, and dense presentation.

The appendix broadens Table 2 and reinforces the paper’s methodological claim: much AI-R&D evaluation remains tied to fixed metrics, executable tests, reference implementations, or model grading. Human-reviewed open-ended systems exist but have different leakage, selection, and evaluation problems. The SEA treats these rows as the authors’ literature synthesis rather than independently verified results.

Evaluation and appraisal

Verdict: Read first. Best use: evaluation-method design, long-horizon agent failure analysis, and building better feedback/budget/context-control loops. Do not use it as a point estimate of general frontier-model research capability or as direct evidence for/against recursive self-improvement timelines.

Main strengths

  • Real, unpublished research questions reduce answer contamination and make the tasks genuinely open-ended.
  • Original authors provide unusually deep task expertise and detailed review rationales.
  • Trajectory evidence connects final failure to process behavior rather than only final-paper scores.
  • The paper discloses researcher priors and multiple design weaknesses unusually explicitly.
  • A second model/scaffold run addresses the simplest “broken scaffold” objection, although only on one task.

Main limitations

  • Two target questions cannot support broad generalization across AI research.
  • Original-author review is high expertise but non-blind and potentially anchored to the authors’ own solution.
  • No positive-control open-ended task establishes whether the method can recognize a genuinely successful autonomous research run.
  • Failure-mode labels depend on interpretation; coauthors themselves disagree on constructs such as creativity versus epistemic lock-in.
  • Robustness is partial: one alternate task/configuration run and no systematic scaffold/model ablation.
  • Claims about reasoning effort improving quality rely on qualitatively different pilots, not a controlled comparison.
Most important overclaim to avoid: “frontier AI agents cannot conduct AI research.” The source supports a narrower claim: the tested systems did not autonomously produce top-conference-quality answers to these two open-ended research questions under the studied setups.

Implementation / research takeaways

Separate generator quality from verifier qualityA critic that detects flaws is insufficient if the agent cannot prioritize or act on those critiques. Evaluation harnesses should measure review-to-action conversion explicitly.
Make backtracking a first-class behaviorTrack whether the system can abandon the project-level framing, not merely rerun a local experiment. Clean-context restart branches are a useful measurable action.
Budget awareness needs policy, not telemetryKnowing remaining tokens, money, GPU hours, and wall-clock time did not yield effective allocation. Harnesses can test policies for spend-to-deadline, stopping, and reserve management.
Instruction persistence is an evaluation targetLong-running agents should be tested for adherence to durable constraints across compaction, resets, and subagent handoffs.
Verify subagent claims at the orchestrator boundaryThe five caught hallucination/misrepresentation incidents suggest that explicit double-checking can prevent subagent errors from reaching final artifacts.
Use shadow evaluations as a complement, not a replacementThey probe rich research judgment that benchmarks miss, but should be paired with verifier-scored tasks, blinded external review, and larger repeated task sets.
